1965-05.summary: 1 RAR's advance guard arrives at Bien Hoa, the start of Australia's commitment of combat troops.
1965-05.text: On 29 April 1965 the Menzies government announced that Australia would provide an infantry battalion for service in Vietnam, in response to a South Vietnamese request made in consultation with the United States[1]. The 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment's (1 RAR's) advance guard reached Bien Hoa on 29 May, and the battalion built up over the following weeks, patrolling first with the US 2/503 Battalion and then on its own. A company and its attachments sailed from Sydney on HMAS Sydney on 27 May, while the rest of the battalion flew[1].

sources.title: Australian infantry serving during the Vietnam War

1965-06.summary: 1 RAR settles in at Bien Hoa, and loses its first men when a grenade goes off by accident.
1965-06.text: The battalion, joined in mid-June by the Prince of Wales Light Horse with its armoured personnel carriers, secured its part of the Bien Hoa Air Base and began patrolling the area around it, firing its first mortar rounds on 25 June and seeing the enemy for the first time on 26 June. That day, after the battalion's first operation, a grenade went off accidentally as a soldier jumped from a truck[1]. Two Australians were killed outright and a third died of his wounds, seven were wounded, and an American was killed and two wounded.

sources.title: Australian infantry serving during the Vietnam War

1965-07.summary: 1 RAR patrols around Bien Hoa and goes out on numbered operations, finding old Viet Cong camps and small groups of the enemy.
1965-07.text: The battalion's tasks were to secure the Bien Hoa air base, patrol deeply and mount offensive operations into the areas around it, and join in operations with American and South Vietnamese troops[1]. Most of July's 33 contacts came on Operation 3/65 (16) and on routine patrols of the battalion's area (14): patrols found and destroyed Viet Cong camps, one built for about 100 men with a hut set up as a lecture theatre, and an old ambush position for 200 to 300 men. Seven of the battalion were recorded wounded, and 4 enemy killed and 8 wounded.

sources.title: Australian infantry serving during the Vietnam War

1965-08.summary: Operation 6/65 and routine patrols: 1 RAR finds and destroys Viet Cong camps, tunnels and a rice cache.
1965-08.text: August's 29 contacts were mostly on Operation 6/65 (19) and the battalion's routine patrols (9), with patrol clashes, sightings and finds of camps in about equal numbers. On 7 August 6 Platoon killed two Viet Cong who threw a grenade when challenged, and over the next two days 4 Platoon destroyed a camp with two tons of rice and a camp of 18 huts with bunkers and tunnels, later struck from the air. Three Australians were recorded wounded, and 4 enemy killed and 5 wounded.

1965-09.summary: Freed from guarding the air base, 1 RAR goes out on search-and-destroy operations, and Australian artillery arrives.
1965-09.text: In September the Australian government lifted the restriction that had kept 1 RAR to defending the air base, and the battalion could be used fully in search-and-destroy, patrolling and security operations[1]. Nearly all the month's 66 contacts came on Operation 10/65, finding and destroying camps and clashing with small local-force groups; one Australian was killed by a sniper and five on the allied side were wounded, and 4 enemy were recorded killed. The 105th Field Battery arrived the same month and fired Australia's first artillery rounds of the war two days after reaching Bien Hoa province[2].

sources.title: Australian Artillery serving during the Vietnam War

1965-10.summary: 1 RAR operates in the Iron Triangle, where mines and booby traps wound many, then on Operation 13/65.
1965-10.text: Most of October's 61 contacts came on Operation 12/65 in the Iron Triangle (33) and Operation 13/65 (10), with 13 on routine tasks. Mines and booby traps (12) and harassing fire (13) were the commonest contacts, and they account for most of the month's 3 friendly killed and 26 wounded. On 25 October, on Operation 13/65, C Company's 8 Platoon fired on 18 Viet Cong crossing a creek and lost a man, and 9 Platoon ambushed a group on a track, killing two; 13 enemy were recorded killed in the month.

1965-11.summary: 1 RAR fights a bunker system on a hilltop on Operation Hump, then clears villages on Operation New Life.
1965-11.text: On Operation Hump (numbered 14/65) the 105th Field Battery became the first Australian battery to be moved by Iroquois helicopter[1]. On 8 November A Company ran into a hill held by at least three dug-in machine-guns and, after two hours, withdrew under fire without two of its men, listed missing believed killed. Later in the month Operation New Life took the battalion into Chanh Duc and Vo Xu villages, detaining many suspects. In all 23 enemy were recorded killed in the month, and the battalion's casualties were 3 killed and 7 wounded.

sources.title: Australian Artillery serving during the Vietnam War

1965-12.summary: A quiet month of searching for rice caches as Operation New Life ends and Operation Smash follows.
1965-12.text: December's 23 contacts were mostly the last of Operation New Life (14) and Operation Smash (7), and most were finds (9 installations) rather than fights: rice caches, huts and a sharpened-stake booby trap, with a Viet Cong who came over to C Company with his shotgun. On 18 December, on Smash, D Company's 12 Platoon met seven Viet Cong and killed two with artillery. Two Australians were recorded wounded.

1966-01.summary: 1 RAR's costliest month: tunnels, snipers and mines on Operation 1/66, including Operation Crimp, and Operation Marauder.
1966-01.text: Most of January's 46 contacts came on Operation 1/66 (32), which included the battalion's part in Operation Crimp in the Hobo Woods north of Saigon, where it uncovered the Cu Chi tunnel complex[1]; the rest came on Operation Marauder (9) and routine tasks. Snipers, command-detonated mines, booby traps and bunkers made it the costliest month of 1 RAR's tour: 7 were recorded killed on the Task Force's side and 10 wounded, and 13 enemy killed.

1966-02.summary: American cavalry seize rice on Operation Roundhouse; 1 RAR guards US engineers on Operation Rolling Stone and ambushes Viet Cong at night.
1966-02.text: February's 50 contacts came on Operation Roundhouse (19), where an American cavalry troop found 60,000 pounds of rice and vehicles, and on Operation 4/66 (23), the battalion's part in Operation Rolling Stone, guarding US Army engineers building a road for the US 1st Infantry Division[1]. On Rolling Stone night ambushes and pickets caught Viet Cong moving around the battalion's positions, and on 24 February a single section's ambush engaged about 28 of them. No Australians were recorded killed and four were wounded, while 17 enemy were recorded killed.

1966-03.summary: 1 RAR spends the month on Operation Silver City across the Song Be, as Australia decides to replace it with a task force.
1966-03.text: On 8 March the Australian government approved the expansion of its force to a task force, to operate independently of the Americans and fight in its own way[1]. The battalion meanwhile spent most of the month on Operation Silver City (50 of 59 contacts), crossing the Song Be and fighting Viet Cong groups guarding rice caches; 2 were recorded killed and 12 wounded on the allied side, and 22 enemy killed. At the end of the month it began Operation Abilene.

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

1966-04.summary: 1 RAR ambushes around Binh Ba on Operation Abilene, then clears rubber and jungle around Song Be on Operation Denver, as 5 RAR arrives.
1966-04.text: April's 59 contacts came on Operation Abilene (31), around the Binh Ba airstrip and rubber plantation, and Operation Denver (23) near Song Be, most of them patrols and night ambushes in which the Viet Cong seldom fired back. No one on the allied side was recorded killed and six were wounded, and 16 enemy were recorded killed and 18 wounded. The same month the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, the first of the task force's new battalions, arrived at the new base at Nui Dat[1].

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

1966-05.summary: 5 RAR's first operation, Hardihood: clearing Long Phuoc and Long Tan and patrolling the ground around the new base at Nui Dat.
1966-05.text: May was the month of Operation Hardihood, in which the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR), with the 1st Battalion (1 RAR) and the US 173rd Airborne Brigade, removed the people of Long Phuoc and Long Tan from around the new base at Nui Dat and resettled them in nearby villages[1]. Hardihood accounts for 32 of the month's 37 contacts, 30 of them 5 RAR's and six 1 RAR's, mostly patrols (15) and ambushes (5) meeting small parties of enemy around the villages. One Australian was killed, on 24 May, shot by his own side during what may have been a contact with the enemy, and 7 enemy were recorded killed; in one of those contacts, on 31 May, a platoon surrounding a hut killed one of three people searching for food and wounded another, who died in the night, and the record notes they were probably civilians.

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

1966-06.summary: Hardihood ends, 6 RAR arrives and begins destroying the emptied village of Long Phuoc, and enemy mortars reach the Australians around the base.
1966-06.text: In June 1 RAR finished its tour and went home, replaced by the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), which from 21 June searched, cleared and destroyed the deserted village of Long Phuoc in Operation Enoggera, because mortar attacks on the Task Force's area had continued[1]. Hardihood went on until 24 June and accounts for 58 of the month's 91 contacts, and Enoggera for 17; 5 RAR had 48 of them and 6 RAR 24, and the Special Air Service appears for the first time. The enemy's mortars were the danger: on 10 June 120 mm and 82 mm fire killed two men of a 5 RAR patrol and wounded four, and two days later another was killed as D Company swept north-east of Hoa Long for the mortar positions. In all 4 were killed on the Task Force's side and 12 wounded, and 11 enemy were recorded killed.

sources.title: Nui Dat base in Phuoc Tuy Province during the Vietnam War

1966-07.summary: Patrols and ambushes close to Nui Dat, the operations named Sydney, and 6 RAR's Hobart, where a battalion cordon met a Viet Cong company.
1966-07.text: July's 94 contacts came mostly from patrols (50) and ambushes (12) close to Nui Dat, 34 of them in the Task Force's routine work around the base, and from the operations named Sydney (Sydney 2 had 16 contacts) and Hobart (13), an operation of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR). Hobart brought the month's sharpest fighting: on 25 July, in a battalion cordon, B Company of 6 RAR fought most of a Viet Cong company and had two killed and twelve wounded, one Australian shell falling short into its position, while C Company met another enemy company nearby and found a large bunker system. Earlier, on 9 July, a half-platoon ambush of 6 RAR only a kilometre outside the base was attacked before dawn and lost a man killed, and the Special Air Service's patrols, with 9 contacts, recorded ambushes of their own. In all 4 were killed on the Task Force's side and 21 wounded, and 48 enemy were recorded killed.

1966-08.summary: A cordon and search at Binh Ba, the shelling of Nui Dat, and the Battle of Long Tan on 18 August.
1966-08.text: August began with Operation Holsworthy, a cordon and search of Binh Ba village from 5 to 18 August in which the Australians apprehended a number of Viet Cong guerrillas and sympathisers, though within two months a Viet Cong cadre was back in the village[1][2]. On the night of 16 and 17 August the base at Nui Dat was shelled, and on 18 August D Company of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), met a far larger force in the Long Tan rubber plantation[3]. The record dates the shelling to 17 August, with one Australian killed and 24 wounded in the artillery lines, and counts 17 Australians killed and 245 enemy killed in the Battle of Long Tan; the month's totals are 19 killed on the Task Force's side and 47 wounded, and 284 enemy killed. Afterwards 5 RAR began Operation Toledo, trying to encircle an enemy force north of the Nui Dinh hills[2].

sources.title: Australians in the Battle of Binh Ba 6 to 7 June 1969

1966-09.summary: Toledo ends and 6 RAR searches the Nui Dinh hills in Operation Vaucluse, meeting small parties of local Viet Cong on the tracks.
1966-09.text: Operation Toledo went on until 8 September[1], and the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), then searched the Nui Dinh hills in Operation Vaucluse, a search-and-destroy operation of 16 days aimed at destroying the enemy's men and bases there[2]. Vaucluse accounts for 15 of the month's 37 contacts and Toledo for 8, mostly patrols (17) and security (9), and the clashes were small, with local Viet Cong: on 14 September 1 Platoon of A Company, astride a track near a company-sized camp, killed two of a party carrying medical supplies, probably to a hospital, and 2 Platoon, following, killed three more. No Australian was killed in the month and one was wounded; 11 enemy were recorded killed.

sources.title: Australian infantry serving during the Vietnam War

1966-10.summary: 5 RAR searches the Nui Thi Vai hills in Canberra and Queanbeyan, among snipers and booby traps, and the Task Force cordons Hoa Long.
1966-10.text: In October the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR), took the war into the Nui Thi Vai and Nui Toc Tien hills in two search-and-destroy operations, Canberra and Queanbeyan, and on 30 October the Task Force cordoned Hoa Long with both battalions while South Vietnamese forces searched it, in Operation Bundaberg, which largely eliminated the Viet Cong organisation in the village[1]. The hills were thick with booby traps and snipers: on 8 October, in Canberra, two booby traps wounded men of C Company, and in Queanbeyan, which accounts for 10 of the month's 47 contacts, three Australians were killed. In all 4 were killed on the Task Force's side and 28 wounded, and 22 enemy were recorded killed, ten of them when 10 Platoon of 5 RAR surrounded two hidden huts on 21 October.

sources.title: The 'Red Rats' and Phuoc Tuy
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

1966-11.summary: Operation Hayman in the mangroves of Long Son Island, and 6 RAR's Ingham along the Song Rai against the D445 Battalion.
1966-11.text: November had two operations: Hayman, a search-and-destroy mission on the edge of the Rung Sat mangrove swamps in the south-west of the province, for which the Task Force's headquarters moved forward onto Long Son Island[1], and Ingham, in which the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), searched along the Song Rai river between Nui Dat and Xuyen Moc for the Viet Cong's D445 Battalion[2]. Ingham accounts for 33 of the month's 73 contacts and Hayman, fought by 5 RAR, for 18; on 11 November in Hayman a platoon of D Company smelt Viet Cong near a mangrove swamp, followed their tracks to a small camp and killed four. Two Australians were killed in the month and 10 wounded, and 26 enemy were recorded killed.

sources.title: The 'Red Rats' and Phuoc Tuy
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

1966-12.summary: Ingham ends with a costly mine blast; otherwise a month of routine patrols and ambushes around the base, with small operations named Duck and Canary.
1966-12.text: Ingham ended on 2 December with a command-detonated mine that killed one Australian of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (6 RAR), and wounded ten. After that December's 35 contacts were mostly the two battalions' patrols (17) and ambushes (8), 14 of them in routine work around the base, with small operations named Duck and Canary. On 5 December 8 Platoon of 6 RAR, moving to a night ambush, found twelve heavily armed Viet Cong eating dinner and killed five, and the Special Air Service's patrols recorded several ambushes and contacts of their own. In all 2 were killed on the Task Force's side and 15 wounded, and 21 enemy were recorded killed.

1967-01.summary: Cordons and searches of Hoa Long and villages north of Nui Dat, patrols through the battalions' areas, and ambushes on the Viet Cong's jungle tracks.
1967-01.text: January began with Operation Caloundra, a cordon and search by the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR), north of Nui Dat, followed by Wollongong, a series of patrols through 5 RAR's area[1]; the Task Force also cordoned and searched the village of Hoa Long, a centre of recent Viet Cong activity, in Operation Camden[2]. The month's 24 contacts were small, mostly patrols (11) and ambushes (6); in Kirribili, at the end of the month, A Company of 5 RAR ambushed parties of Viet Cong on a jungle track complex on successive nights, men of the well-trained Chau Duc C20 Company among them. One Australian was wounded, in a Special Air Service patrol's contact, and 13 enemy were recorded killed.

1967-02.summary: A week of heavy losses: a booby trap in a cordon and search, the fight at Ap My An in Operation Bribie, and the Long Hai minefield in Renmark.
1967-02.text: Most of February's 63 contacts were small, 18 of them in Operation Tambourine, but in one week three operations cost the Task Force dearly: on 14 February a booby trap, probably laid by friendly forces, killed three men of C Company headquarters of the 5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5 RAR), in a cordon and search (Beaumaris); on 17 February the 6th Battalion (6 RAR), flown in to cut off a force withdrawing from an attack on Phuoc Hai, ran into a dug-in D445 Battalion position and had eight men killed (Bribie); and on 21 February a carrier taking 5 RAR's B Company towards the Long Hai hills hit a mine, and men running to help set off more, with nine killed (Renmark). In all 20 were killed on the Task Force's side and 62 wounded, more than in the month of Long Tan, and 69 enemy were recorded killed. These losses shocked the small Australian force and fed the thinking of senior officers who believed a third battalion and tanks were needed[1].

sources.title: Australian Armoured units serving during the Vietnam War

1967-03.summary: 5 RAR sets up on the Horseshoe as work begins on the barrier minefield, and 6 RAR, in Portsea, catches a main-force battalion withdrawing across the Song Rai.
1967-03.text: 5 RAR was given the task of setting up a base on the Horseshoe to deny the Viet Cong supplies[1], and work began on the barrier fence and minefield (Leeton), while 6 RAR, with armoured personnel carriers, went out in Portsea to intercept enemy withdrawing from an attack on Lo Gom and fought the rear of 2 Battalion, 275 Regiment, on 21 and 22 March. Of the month's 55 contacts, 38 have no operation recorded, and 26 are recorded against the Task Force as a whole rather than a battalion. The record counts 2 killed on the Task Force's side and 7 wounded, and 16 enemy killed.

1967-04.summary: A month of patrols and ambushes as the fence goes up; mines are the main danger, and Special Air Service ambushes account for many of the enemy killed.
1967-04.text: Portsea ended early in the month and the minefield work went on, but most of April's 76 contacts (60) have no operation recorded. Mines were the danger: one killed a soldier of 6 RAR crossing Route 23, another a soldier of 5 RAR north of Phuoc Loi, and a third killed two of 5 RAR just outside a swept lane. Special Air Service patrols set several ambushes, one of which killed five of the 15 enemy recorded killed this month; and 7 RAR, which began arriving in April to relieve 5 RAR[1], has its first contact.

1967-05.summary: The second rotation takes over: 7 RAR opens with Lismore and 2 RAR replaces 6 RAR, while engineers laying the barrier minefield suffer deadly mine accidents.
1967-05.text: 7 RAR opened with Lismore early in the month (20 contacts of patrols and small clashes around enemy camps), and 2 RAR took over from 6 RAR[1]. The laying of the barrier minefield cost the engineers dearly: mine accidents on 9, 20 and 30 May killed engineers and wounded others, the last of them recorded as friendly fire. 4th Field Regiment's artillery appears in the record (10 contacts), and of the month's 135 contacts 94 have no operation recorded; the record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 12 wounded, and 19 enemy killed.

1967-06.summary: The new battalions patrol in small operations; the artillery of 4th Field Regiment is recorded in more contacts than any other unit.
1967-06.text: With 6 RAR gone home to Brisbane[1], 7 RAR patrolled in Broken Hill (10 contacts) and 2 RAR appears in the record for the first time. The unit most often recorded in contact was not the infantry but the artillery of 4th Field Regiment, with 30 contacts (27 as the unit in contact), ahead of 7 RAR (11) and the Special Air Service (9), whose patrols fought several ambushes and running fights. Of the month's 128 contacts, 100 have no operation recorded; the record counts 3 wounded on the Task Force's side and none killed, and 20 enemy killed.

1967-07.summary: A quieter month of small operations, Cairns and Paddington, with 4th Field Regiment's artillery again the unit most often in contact.
1967-07.text: The small operations Cairns (6 contacts) and Paddington (5) were under way, and Special Air Service patrols ambushed and were lifted out. Again 4th Field Regiment's artillery is recorded in the most contacts, 26, all as the unit in contact, against 7 for 2 RAR. On 20 July mortars shelled a troop of armoured personnel carriers at Duc Thanh, wounding four. The record counts no Australians killed and 5 wounded, and 15 enemy killed.

1967-08.summary: 7 RAR fights the 274th Regiment at Suoi Chau Pha during Ballarat, and mines hit 2 RAR's patrols.
1967-08.text: On 6 August, in Ballarat, A Company of 7 RAR fought the Viet Cong 274th Regiment at Suoi Chau Pha[1], a contact in which the record counts six Australians killed. Mines hit 2 RAR in Cairns and Ulmarra, killing two and wounding three in a company-sized enemy camp west of Hoi My, and wounding six in a minefield north of My An. 4th Field Regiment's artillery was again recorded in the most contacts (34), and the month's 110 contacts count 9 killed on the Task Force's side and 36 wounded, and 33 enemy killed.

sources.title: Combat experiences during the Vietnam War

1967-09.summary: Families are moved to Suoi Nghe in Ainslie while both battalions search the country around; an ambush at the Horseshoe kills three Australians.
1967-09.text: Most of the month's operation contacts were in Ainslie (27), in which Vietnamese families were resettled at Ap Suoi Nghe to deny the Viet Cong supplies[1], while 2 RAR and 7 RAR searched the enemy's camps. On 2 September an old M16 mine killed a New Zealander of V Company, the New Zealand rifle company attached to 2 RAR[2]; on 30 September an enemy squad ambushed a C Company, 2 RAR vehicle at the Horseshoe with Claymore mines, killing three Australians and, later, an interpreter. 4th Field Regiment's artillery was recorded in 30 of the month's 97 contacts; the record counts 4 killed on the Task Force's side and 13 enemy killed.

1967-10.summary: Ambushes in Kenmore kill Viet Cong guerrillas and tax collectors; a 2 RAR ambush near Long Tan kills four unarmed civilians; Santa Fe begins.
1967-10.text: The month's work was mostly patrols (18) and ambushes (5): in Kenmore, early in the month, 7 RAR's ambushes killed men believed to be Xuyen Moc guerrillas and two tax collectors, and 2 RAR found a camp of ten huts. On 23 October a 2 RAR ambush in the prohibited zone north of Long Tan fired on 16 Vietnamese, killing four and wounding six, who proved to be unarmed civilians. Santa Fe began on 28 October. Of 53 contacts, the record counts 2 wounded on the Task Force's side and 22 enemy killed.

1967-11.summary: Santa Fe and then Forrest bring the heaviest fighting since the new battalions arrived, with night attacks on Australian positions and a costly assault on a base camp.
1967-11.text: Most of November's 97 contacts were in Santa Fe (44), in the north-east of the province[1], and, from 25 November, Forrest (12). The enemy fired Claymore mines into 108 Field Battery's position and into a 7 RAR platoon's base at night, and on 27 November D Company of 7 RAR attacked a base camp and was counter-attacked, with two killed and 22 wounded, while a booby trap and a command-detonated mine hit 2 RAR. The record counts 9 killed on the Task Force's side and 43 wounded, and 56 enemy killed.

sources.title: Operation Santa Fe, north-east of Phuoc Tuy Province, November 1967 (COL/67/1120/VN)

1967-12.summary: Forrest's ambushes catch parties of Viet Cong carrying food; two Australian advisers are killed in an ambush, and 3 RAR arrives.
1967-12.text: Forrest went on through the month (31 contacts), mostly ambushes of small Viet Cong parties carrying food and packs, among them a Special Air Service ambush that killed seven on 12 December. On 16 December two Australian advisers and four South Vietnamese soldiers were killed when their vehicle was ambushed. The 3rd Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (3 RAR) arrived during December and brought the Task Force to three battalions[1]; it appears in 2 of the month's 92 contacts. The record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 4 wounded, and 26 enemy killed.

1968-01.summary: Duntroon and Forrest, then Coburg: the Task Force is sent out of Phuoc Tuy for the first time as the Tet offensive nears.
1968-01.text: January 1968 began with Operations Duntroon (21 contacts) and Forrest (17), and ended with the Task Force's first deployment outside Phuoc Tuy, Operation Coburg, on the Bien Hoa–Long Khanh border from 24 January[1]. The record has 147 contacts, 48 of them on Coburg, most by 2 RAR (44) and 7 RAR (33), mostly on patrol (58), in ambush (23) or on security (22), with 22 counted as routine work. In the last week, as 2 RAR and 7 RAR ran into enemy camps on Coburg, the fighting grew heavy: 7 were killed on the Task Force's side and 45 wounded in the month, and 95 enemy recorded killed.

1968-02.summary: The Tet offensive: Coburg in Bien Hoa, and 3 RAR fighting to clear Ba Ria and Long Dien.
1968-02.text: The Tet offensive broke on 31 January, and D445 Battalion seized Ba Ria in the early hours of 1 February[1]. 3 RAR, carried in the carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment, fought to clear the town, and on 8 February helped the South Vietnamese clear Long Dien, while 2 RAR and 7 RAR, and later 3 RAR, fought on in Operation Coburg (93 contacts this month), where Fire Support Base Anderson was attacked on 18 February. The record has 159 contacts in the month, with 16 killed on the Task Force's side and 92 wounded, and 218 enemy recorded killed and 50 wounded.

sources.title: Tet Offensive, Operation Coburg and the Battle of Ba Ria 1968

1968-03.summary: Operation Pinnaroo in the Long Hai hills, with mines taking a heavy toll and tanks in action for the first time.
1968-03.text: March was the month of Operation Pinnaroo in the Long Hai hills (72 contacts), where mines and booby traps caused most of the Task Force's losses and 3 RAR worked with carriers and tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment, which went into action for the first time on Pinnaroo[1]. Outside it the record has 18 contacts of routine work and 59 not assigned to an operation, among them an SAS patrol's ambush on 18 March that blew up a tractor and trailer carrying ammunition, with 21 enemy recorded killed. In all there were 151 contacts, with 6 killed on the Task Force's side and 47 wounded, and 58 enemy recorded killed.

sources.title: Australian Armoured units serving during the Vietnam War

1968-04.summary: 1 RAR takes over from 7 RAR; Pinnaroo ends, and the Task Force joins Operation Toan Thang 1 on the Bien Hoa border.
1968-04.text: 1 RAR arrived for its second tour and relieved 7 RAR on 9 April[1]. Pinnaroo ended on 11 April, 2 RAR patrolled and ambushed near Hoa Long in Operation Cook Town Orchid (17 contacts), where mines and booby traps wounded its New Zealanders, and in the last week the Task Force joined Operation Toan Thang 1 (21 contacts); SAS patrols had 15 contacts. It was a quieter month, with 91 contacts, 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 19 wounded, and 43 enemy recorded killed.

1968-05.summary: The Battle of Coral–Balmoral: 1 RAR and 3 RAR hold fire support bases north of Saigon against North Vietnamese attacks.
1968-05.text: Almost the whole month's fighting (114 of 124 contacts) was in Operation Toan Thang 1, where 1 RAR and 3 RAR, sent north of Saigon to intercept enemy forces withdrawing from it, held Fire Support Bases Coral and Balmoral against attacks by North Vietnamese battalions[1]. Coral was attacked on 13 and 16 May and Balmoral on 26 and 28 May, and tanks and infantry fought into bunker systems outside the wire. In the month 29 were killed on the Task Force's side and 115 wounded, and 267 enemy recorded killed and 85 wounded.

sources.title: Australians in the Battle of Coral–Balmoral 12 May to 6 June 1968

1968-06.summary: The Task Force leaves Coral and Balmoral; 4 RAR replaces 2 RAR, and SAS patrols carry much of the month's fighting.
1968-06.text: Coral was closed on 6 June and 1 RAR returned to Nui Dat, and 4 RAR relieved 2 RAR on 1 June[1][2]. The record has only 45 contacts, most by SAS patrols (11), with Toan Thang 1 (9) giving way to Toan Thang 2 (6), where 3 RAR and armour destroyed sampans running a shuttle service across a river, and Operation Kosciusko (5). Two Australians were killed and 10 wounded, and 37 enemy recorded killed.

1968-07.summary: Merino, and a busy month for the SAS.
1968-07.text: July 1968's main operation was Merino (29 of the month's 59 contacts), in which 4 RAR fought over enemy bunker systems in its last days. The SAS had 13 contacts: on 5 July a six-man patrol of 2 SAS Squadron killed 13 of more than 25 enemy without loss, and on 11 July another killed five Viet Cong, one of whom carried an award for the best soldier of D445 Battalion in 1966. Mines took their toll, killing a soldier of 1 RAR clearing a landing zone on 9 July and hitting armoured personnel carriers ambushed in thick jungle on 15 July. The record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 18 wounded, and 50 enemy killed.

1968-08.summary: Platypus and Lyre Bird in the jungle, and a Viet Cong attack on Long Dien.
1968-08.text: August 1968 began with Platypus (33 contacts), in which 1 RAR and 3 RAR met mines and defended bunker systems, while 4 RAR guarded the engineers clearing trails in Lyre Bird (20). On 22 August about 100 enemy of D445 Battalion's C1 Company attacked Long Dien and were driven out by 1 RAR with tanks, carriers and helicopter gunships. Patrols (37) and security tasks (18) were most of the month's 91 contacts. The record counts 8 killed on the Task Force's side and 47 wounded, and 76 enemy killed.

1968-09.summary: Hawkesbury on the Long Khanh–Bien Hoa border; 3 RAR guards the towns.
1968-09.text: September 1968 was dominated by Hawkesbury (40 of 74 contacts), in which 4 RAR and 1 RAR ambushed enemy supply parties and fought over bunker systems; its worst day was 13 September, when a 4 RAR platoon lost three killed attacking a system of 20 interlocking bunkers. Nearer home, 3 RAR's B and D Companies took over the defence of Ba Ria and Long Dien in Nowra[1]. On 3 September a 2 SAS Squadron patrol fired on a Popular Forces company under US command that had wandered into its area, wounding seven of its men and a US adviser, a friendly-fire incident. The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 18 wounded, and 64 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

1968-10.summary: Windsor and Capital: 3 RAR's last full month of operations, and many ambushes.
1968-10.text: In October 1968 3 RAR, in its last full month, had 36 of the 96 contacts, moving from Windsor into Capital and then Harvest[1]. Ambushes (34) and patrols (33) were the bulk of the work, and the SAS had 15 contacts, among them patrols that killed eight enemy with their ox-carts on 5 October and seven more on 23 October. Two bunker fights on 8 October each cost two Australian lives, one in Windsor and one in Track Duster, where a 4 RAR platoon was hit by a mine made from a mortar shell. The record counts 9 killed on the Task Force's side and 27 wounded, and 110 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

1968-11.summary: 9 RAR arrives and 3 RAR goes home; 1 RAR and 4 RAR work through Capital 2.
1968-11.text: In November 1968 9 RAR arrived at Nui Dat, and on 20 November 3 RAR sailed for Australia[1]. In the field, 1 RAR and 4 RAR worked through Capital 2 (35 of the month's 74 contacts), which ended on 24 November with an attack on a bunker complex in which a platoon commander and a section commander of 1 RAR were killed. On 21 November a reaction force of tanks, carriers and a 3 RAR platoon went to Ap Ngai Giao, occupied by about 20 enemy. The record counts 7 killed on the Task Force's side and 12 wounded, and 38 enemy killed.

sources.title: The 3RAR in South Vietnam – First Tour 1967/1968

1968-12.summary: Goodwood begins, against a feared Viet Cong offensive; 1 RAR fights through bunker systems.
1968-12.text: Goodwood began on 3 December 1968, a reaction to an increase in Viet Cong activity that suggested an offensive was being planned[1][2]. It took 80 of the month's 118 contacts, and 1 RAR had most of them (48), fighting bunker systems in which claymores fired by a few defenders did much of the damage: on 19 December two claymores killed one of a 1 RAR platoon and wounded nine or ten. Patrols (50) and security tasks (25) were the month's routine. The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 45 wounded, and 71 enemy killed.

1969-01.summary: 9 RAR joins Goodwood and is the unit most often in contact, meeting costly fights in enemy bunker systems.
1969-01.text: 9 RAR joined Goodwood on 1 January 1969[1]. It was the unit most often in contact that month (55 of 147 contacts), and Goodwood took 120 of them. The new battalion learned in bunker fights: on 6 January a sentry's claymore killed two of a 9 RAR platoon, on 10 January another platoon fought a bunker system for three and a half hours, and on 19 January a single rocket-propelled grenade killed three men gathered for orders. On 29 January W Company, 4 RAR, led by the SAS into an enemy infiltration area, fought off part of an enemy company in a night ambush. The record counts 14 killed on the Task Force's side and 49 wounded, and 96 enemy killed.

1969-02.summary: Goodwood ends and Federal begins in Bien Hoa after the 1969 Tet offensive; 5 RAR relieves 1 RAR.
1969-02.text: February 1969 saw the end of Goodwood (57 contacts) and the start of Federal (30), searches and patrols in Bien Hoa province after the 1969 Tet offensive[1]; 5 RAR relieved 1 RAR on 15 February[2]. On 16 February tanks and B Company, 4 RAR, attacked a bunker system, losing two killed and eight wounded, and on the night of 23 February W Company, 4 RAR, covering the approaches to Long Binh, beat off several attacks. The record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 32 wounded, and 94 enemy killed.

1969-03.summary: Federal continues in Bien Hoa; 5 RAR is now the unit most often in contact, and an advisory team is caught near Dat Do.
1969-03.text: In March 1969 Federal went on (42 of the month's 88 contacts), and 5 RAR was now the unit most often in contact (33). Quintus Thrust had 18 contacts; in one, on 4 March, a 5 RAR ambush killed men thought, from the money they carried, to be tax collectors. On 7 March a 4 RAR Mobile Advisory Team ambushing with Regional Force soldiers near Dat Do was caught in the open paddy, and an Australian corporal and three Vietnamese were killed. On 27 March two trucks of a US convoy escorted by Australians hit mines on Route 15. The record counts 4 killed and 27 wounded on the allied side, and 62 enemy killed.

1969-04.summary: The Task Force makes pacification its first priority; 9 RAR's Overlander, then Stafford and Surfside.
1969-04.text: In April 1969 the Task Force made pacification its first priority: seeking out and destroying the enemy in its base areas, keeping him from the civilian population and helping create a secure climate for South Vietnamese life[1]. The month's biggest operation was Overlander (60 of 133 contacts), mostly 9 RAR's, followed by 4 RAR's Stafford and 5 RAR's Surfside. Bunker fights (14) were still costly: on 4 April a 5 RAR platoon lost two killed and seven wounded in four hours, and on 8 April 9 RAR's D Company cleared 25 bunkers after one of its platoons was hit. The record counts 7 killed on the Task Force's side and 61 wounded, and 84 enemy killed.

1969-05.summary: 6 RAR replaces 4 RAR; 5 RAR's Twickenham and 9 RAR's Reynella, and a busy month for the armour.
1969-05.text: In May 1969 6 RAR arrived to relieve 4 RAR, and was joined by a New Zealand company to become 6RAR/NZ (ANZAC) Battalion[1]. 5 RAR's Twickenham and 9 RAR's Reynella took 30 of the month's 137 contacts each, and the tanks of the 1st Armoured Regiment and the carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment had 16 each: on 29 May a combined ambush of carriers and infantry at the ruins of Thua Tich village on Route 328 killed 11 of about 50 enemy. On 15 May a reaction force went with 9 RAR to Dat Do, where South Vietnamese troops had been fighting an enemy company since morning. The record counts 6 killed on the Task Force's side and 60 wounded, and 76 enemy killed.

1969-06.summary: The busiest month of the year: 6 RAR's Lavarack defeats a North Vietnamese incursion, the Battle of Binh Ba, and mines around Dat Do.
1969-06.text: June 1969 had more contacts (173) than any other month of the year, and 6 RAR's Lavarack took 78 of them, as the battalion drove 33 North Vietnamese Regiment out of the province and ambushed 274 Viet Cong Regiment's supply routes[1]. At Binh Ba on 6 and 7 June the Task Force's ready reaction force, with tanks and carriers, cleared North Vietnamese troops from the village house by house (Operation Hammer)[2]. Mines around Dat Do cost 5 RAR dearly in ESSO: on 15 June a single mine killed three and wounded 20 to 24. The record counts 14 killed on the Task Force's side and 92 wounded, and 252 enemy killed.

sources.title: Operation Lavarack: Phuoc Tuy Province, Vietnam, 1969
sources.publisher: Australian Army Journal (Australian Army Research Centre)

sources.title: Australians in the Battle of Binh Ba 6 to 7 June 1969

1969-07.summary: A month of mines: 6 RAR and 5 RAR lose men to M16 mines in the south-east of the province, and 16 are killed in all.
1969-07.text: July 1969 was a month of mines. 6 RAR was on Operation Mundingburra (32 contacts), where M16 mines struck again and again, among them one near Hoi My on 21 July that killed a platoon commander and wounded 18; on 5 RAR's Operation Esso (17), mines on the edge of the Long Hai hills killed three and wounded 14 on 4 July, and a 9 RAR platoon lost a man killed and eight wounded attacking a bunker system on 19 July. The Task Force's guns also helped local forces at Thai Thien beat off an attack by 40 to 50 enemy on 9 July, and 14 Viet Cong were recorded killed. In all 109 contacts, mostly patrols (39) and ambushes (21), cost 16 Australian and New Zealand soldiers killed and 87 wounded, with 63 enemy recorded killed.

1969-08.summary: 5 RAR's Operation Camden dominates the month, and a single counter-attack on 21 August wounds more than 30 Australians.
1969-08.text: In August 1969 5 RAR's Operation Camden, north of Nui Dat, dominated the record (47 contacts), and its worst day came on 21 August in the action recorded as Camden 2: an assault on a bunker system was driven back, and a large enemy force counter-attacked the base as the wounded were being flown out, leaving one Australian killed and more than 30 wounded. Near the beach on 5 August, four armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment lying in ambush caught 20 to 25 enemy, and 13 were recorded killed. Security tasks (33 contacts) were almost as common as patrols (39) and ambushes (29), and 6 RAR finished Operation Mundingburra. The month's 143 contacts cost 8 killed and 93 wounded, and 106 enemy were recorded killed.

1969-09.summary: A quieter month of bunker searches by 5 RAR and 6 RAR, while a 9 RAR advisory team helps defend Dat Do.
1969-09.text: September 1969 was quieter: 108 contacts, with 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 25 wounded, and 71 enemy recorded killed. 6 RAR was on Operation Burnham (26) and 5 RAR on Operation Kingston (16), finding and attacking the enemy's bunker camps, and SAS patrols were in contact 10 times. With the start of the American withdrawals, the Task Force's emphasis had shifted towards training the South Vietnamese Regional and Popular Forces[1]. At Dat Do on 4 September, enemy who got past the Regional Force bunkers ran into a small mobile advisory team from 9 RAR's B Company, which held them off through the night with a Spooky gunship's help until they withdrew at first light.

1969-10.summary: 9 RAR ambushes around Thai Thien on Operation Jack, and 6 RAR begins Operation Ross along the Song Rai.
1969-10.text: In October 1969 9 RAR was the busiest battalion, with 45 contacts, most of them on Operation Jack (39), where its ambushes near Thai Thien caught enemy slipping in behind civilians returning to the village and A Company ambushed a group of 50 to 60 on the night of 24 October. 6 RAR began Operation Ross (18) and 5 RAR finished Kingston (7). On 22 October two rocket-propelled grenades hit an armoured personnel carrier working with 6 RAR, and on 25 October an M16 mine north of Lo Gom killed two Australians and wounded six. The month's 115 contacts cost 7 killed and 18 wounded, and 57 enemy were recorded killed.

1969-11.summary: 5 RAR's Operation Kings Cross, with the carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment, fills the month; 8 RAR arrives and relieves 9 RAR.
1969-11.text: November 1969 belonged to 5 RAR's Operation Kings Cross (72 contacts), fought around the enemy's bunker systems with the armoured personnel carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (22 contacts in the month); on 2 November carrier-borne C Company killed six enemy in a swamp and a B Company platoon ambushing a bunker system's approach killed five. The carriers also worked with the province's own troops, helping a Regional Force platoon attack a bunker complex on 19 November, and on 21 November a carrier section and two platoons from the Task Force's headquarters ambushed and killed six enemy. The 8th Battalion arrived in Vietnam on 17 November and relieved 9 RAR on 25 November[1]. The month's 141 contacts cost 5 killed and 34 wounded, with 77 enemy recorded killed.

1969-12.summary: All three battalions in the field: 6 RAR on Marsden, the newly arrived 8 RAR on Atherton, and 5 RAR finishing Kings Cross.
1969-12.text: In December 1969 all three battalions were in the field: 6 RAR on Operation Marsden (47 contacts), 8 RAR on the first weeks of Operation Atherton (36) and 5 RAR finishing Kings Cross (12). The bunker fighting was costly: on 7 December tanks and carriers had to come to the help of a 5 RAR platoon outflanked at a bunker system, and on 21 December an 8 RAR company assaulted six bunkers for 2 hours 40 minutes and lost a man killed. On 8 December an armoured personnel carrier near Thua Tich set off three anti-tank mines, killing two, and the helicopter sent for the wounded landed on another. The month's 144 contacts cost 10 killed and 50 wounded, and 73 enemy were recorded killed.

1970-01.summary: A month of ambushes by three battalions and the SAS, with 93 enemy recorded killed against four Australians.
1970-01.text: January 1970 was a month of ambushes (42 of its 139 contacts) and patrols (46): 6 RAR was on Operation Napier (33), 5 RAR on Bondi (24) and 8 RAR finished Atherton (13). On 13 January an 8 RAR patrol ambushing a track junction by the Suoi Hoa Nuoc waited for a radio it could hear to reach its killing ground, and of 11 enemy eight were killed and two captured; SAS patrols' ambushes killed five on 9 January and seven on 11 January. Mines went on taking their toll: on 30 January one killed two engineers and wounded four with 6 RAR's A Company. In all 4 were killed on the Task Force's side and 18 wounded, and 93 enemy were recorded killed.

1970-02.summary: 8 RAR's Operation Hammersley in the Long Hai hills brings heavy losses, and 5 RAR's tour ends as 7 RAR arrives.
1970-02.text: February 1970 was costly: 11 killed and 97 wounded in 140 contacts, with 91 enemy recorded killed. The heaviest losses came on 8 RAR's Operation Hammersley in the Long Hai hills (37 contacts), where on 18 February C Company, with carriers and tanks, attacked a bunker system said by a prisoner to hold about 40 enemy, and on 28 February a single M16 jumping mine killed seven men of an A Company platoon and wounded 13. 6 RAR carried on with Napier (27) and at the end of the month began Operation Gisborne against the new base of D445 Battalion, while 5 RAR ended its tour with Bondi (15). The 7th Battalion returned to Vietnam in February 1970, relieving 5 RAR[1].

1970-03.summary: 7 RAR back for a second tour; 6 RAR/NZ and 8 RAR in hard bunker and mine fighting; 6 killed, 38 wounded, 34 enemy recorded killed.
1970-03.text: In February 1970 7 RAR had returned for its second tour, relieving 5 RAR[1]. Of the month's 110 contacts, the most were in Finschhafen (21), Gisborne (11) and Hamilton (7), with 52 under no operation; guarding positions (33), patrols (21) and artillery and mortar fire (19) led the tasks. It was a costly month: on 6 March an M16 mine south of Xuyen Moc killed two of 8 RAR and wounded six, on 8 March D Company of 6 RAR/NZ lost three killed attacking bunkers, and on 19 March a New Zealand soldier was killed when 30 to 50 Viet Cong fired from a bunker system. The record counts 6 killed and 38 wounded, and 34 enemy recorded killed.

1970-04.summary: Townsville, Concrete and Phoi Hop, and the government's announcement that 8 RAR would not be replaced: 115 contacts, 76 enemy recorded killed, 10 killed on the Task Force's side.
1970-04.text: On 20 April the United States announced it would withdraw 150,000 troops over the next 12 months, and two days later the Prime Minister, John Gorton, announced that 8 RAR would not be replaced when its tour ended in November 1970[1]. In the province the month's 115 contacts were mostly ambushes (40) and patrols (35), in Townsville (26), Concrete (25) and Phoi Hop (14), with 7 RAR (32) and 8 RAR (23) most often in contact and the Special Air Service Regiment's patrols (13) busy. Concrete opened with an armoured personnel carrier mined off Route 23 and a fierce fight at bunkers along the Song Rai, and on 25 April a 7 RAR ambush met more than 50 enemy. The record counts 10 killed and 53 wounded, and 76 enemy recorded killed and 41 wounded.

sources.title: Withdrawal of Australian personnel from Vietnam War 1971 to 1973

1970-05.summary: 2 RAR/NZ replaced 6 RAR; 7 RAR's Concrete and 8 RAR's Nudgee ambushes kept up the pressure: 117 contacts, 68 enemy recorded killed.
1970-05.text: In May 2 RAR relieved 6 RAR at Nui Dat and, with two New Zealand companies, took the title 2 RAR/NZ (ANZAC) on 15 May[1]. The month's 117 contacts were mostly ambushes (33) and patrols (30), in Concrete (33), Nudgee (26) and Capricorn (9), with 7 RAR (28) and 8 RAR (27) most often in contact and the tanks and carriers busy in support. 8 RAR's ambushes in the paddy fields near Dat Do drew repeated counter-attacks, and on 21 May two 7 RAR platoons with tanks and carriers fought into an occupied bunker system, losing one killed and 12 wounded. The record counts 4 killed and 59 wounded, and 68 enemy recorded killed and 58 wounded.

1970-06.summary: Operation Cung Chung began on 12 June: intensive patrolling and ambushing to keep the enemy from the villages. Mines and bunkers cost 7 killed.
1970-06.text: On 12 June the Task Force began Operation Cung Chung, intensive patrolling and ambushing to deter the enemy from moving through the area[1]. The month's 102 contacts were mostly ambushes (25), guarding positions (23) and patrols (19), in Cung Chung (30, with 13 more under Cung Chung 1), Capricorn (15) and the end of Concrete (5). Mines and bunkers were the danger: on 6 June an M16 mine laid on the likely line of a 7 RAR follow-up killed three, and on 18 June a New Zealand platoon of 2 RAR/NZ was hit by a command-detonated shell at a bunker system. The record counts 7 killed and 23 wounded, and 30 enemy recorded killed.

1970-07.summary: 7 RAR ambushed around Dat Do in Birdwood while 2 RAR/NZ worked through caves and bunkers in Nathan; no Australians killed, 36 wounded.
1970-07.text: July's 77 contacts were mostly ambushes (26) and patrols (19), in Birdwood (21), 7 RAR's ambushing around Dat Do and Long Phuoc Hai, Nathan (20), 2 RAR/NZ's, and Petrie (10). Mines and booby traps caused most of the wounds: a carrier of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment hit a pressure mine west of Cam My on 6 July, and on 26 July a New Zealand platoon was attacked among caves and then hit by command-detonated mines. No Australians were killed and 36 were wounded; 39 enemy were recorded killed.

1970-08.summary: The second phase of Cung Chung: 8 RAR's ambush outside Hoa Long killed 19 Viet Cong, and a booby-trapped shell wounded two commanding officers.
1970-08.text: August's 55 contacts were mostly in the second phase of Cung Chung (29), with patrols (21) and ambushes (15) the main tasks and 2 RAR (21) most often in contact. On 2 August a booby-trapped 155mm shell in a bunker system killed two men and wounded two commanding officers, and on 29 August a carrier fitted with new belly armour was thrown onto a tank by a mine, its hull unpierced. On 12 August 8 RAR's ambush of Route 2 outside Hoa Long killed 19 Viet Cong and captured six. The record counts 3 killed and 29 wounded, and 45 enemy recorded killed.

1970-09.summary: A quieter month of patrols and ambushes as Cung Chung's second phase gave way to its third: 38 contacts, 21 enemy recorded killed, one Australian wounded.
1970-09.text: September was quieter: 38 contacts, mostly patrols (17) and ambushes (11), as the second phase of Operation Cung Chung (10) gave way to the third (11) on 11 September. The ambushes still paid: on 17 September 7 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon killed four enemy on a track near Dat Do, and on 28 September a New Zealand patrol of 2 RAR/NZ killed five Viet Cong. 21 enemy were recorded killed and 10 wounded; one Australian was wounded and none killed.

1970-10.summary: 8 RAR's last month of operations; Cung Chung's patrols and ambushes went on, with a fabricated contact report among them.
1970-10.text: 8 RAR ceased operations in October, ahead of going home unreplaced[1]; its last contact in the record was an ambush on Route 2 on 9 October that killed four Viet Cong and captured a North Vietnamese soldier. Almost all the month's 28 contacts were in the third phase of Cung Chung (20), patrols (11) and ambushes (8) among them; on 8 October a 2 RAR platoon following a fresh track was caught in the open by 20 to 30 enemy digging in, losing one killed. On 31 October a New Zealand soldier was killed and two wounded in what was reported as a contact at a river crossing; the official history records that the casualties were caused by an accidental discharge of the platoon's own machine-gun and the report was fabricated. The record counts 2 killed and 5 wounded, and 11 enemy recorded killed.

1970-11.summary: 8 RAR went home unreplaced, leaving two battalions; 7 RAR and 2 RAR/NZ kept up Cung Chung's patrols and ambushes, with 12 enemy recorded killed.
1970-11.text: 8 RAR reached home on 12 November 1970; it was not replaced, and the Task Force fell to two battalions[1]. The month's 40 contacts were nearly all in Cung Chung's third phase (27), patrols (18) and ambushes (10), by 7 RAR (14), 2 RAR (7) and the Special Air Service Regiment's patrols (6). The ambushes met small parties: a prisoner taken on 4 November said his group had been going to collect rice, and on 27 November a 7 RAR patrol killed two of the Long Dat unit. No Australians were killed and 5 were wounded; 12 enemy were recorded killed.

1970-12.summary: The first month with two battalions: 2 RAR and 7 RAR ambushing in Cung Chung 3, ending with a large ambush of D445 Battalion on New Year's Eve.
1970-12.text: With 8 RAR gone home in November and not replaced, the Task Force now had two battalions[1]. 2 RAR (14 contacts) and 7 RAR (11) worked on in Cung Chung 3 (29 of the month's 43 contacts), mostly by ambush (16) and patrol (13), with carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment in support. On 15 December an ambush of 2 RAR covering the house of a known Viet Cong food supplier killed 10 enemy, and on 31 December about 45 Viet Cong walked into an ambush of B Company, 7 RAR, and the 3rd Cavalry Regiment: 21 were killed, among them the second-in-command and political officer of D445 Battalion, and documents of strategic value were taken. The record counts 1 killed on the Task Force's side and 15 wounded, and 51 enemy killed.

1971-01.summary: Cung Chung 3 continued: 7 RAR and 2 RAR ambushing Viet Cong food parties around the villages and the Long Hai hills.
1971-01.text: Cung Chung 3 continued (29 of 46 contacts), and ambushes were half the month's work (22). 7 RAR's ambushes near the Long Hai hills met parties of about 20 enemy, and each cost an Australian killed; 2 RAR's platoons ambushed food parties at houses in the rubber at night, killing five on 22 January and five on 31 January. On 17 January a mine on Route 329 killed a Vietnamese Bushman Scout and wounded seven Australians riding on a carrier. The record counts 3 killed and 22 wounded on the Task Force's side, and 35 enemy killed.

1971-02.summary: Phoi Hop began, 7 RAR's tour ended, and mines caused most of the month's casualties.
1971-02.text: Operation Phoi Hop began (26 of the month's 38 contacts), with 2 RAR in contact most often (16). On 25 February HMAS Sydney landed 3 RAR at Vung Tau and took 7 RAR home[1]. Mines caused most of the casualties: an M16 mine in a 7 RAR ambush position south of Xuyen Moc on 1 February (two died of their wounds), a mine under a Land Rover at the Cam My rubber, two mines on a 2 RAR patrol, and an anti-tank mine under a carrier in the Cam My rubber. The record counts 3 killed on the Task Force's side and 13 wounded, and 10 enemy killed.

1971-03.summary: The busiest month of the year: 3 RAR's first operation, Briar Patch, against D445 Battalion, while 2 RAR continued Phoi Hop.
1971-03.text: With 104 contacts this was the busiest month of the Task Force's last year. The newly arrived 3 RAR (42 contacts) began Briar Patch (44) in the north-east of the province, while 2 RAR (19) continued Phoi Hop (31). It was a costly start for 3 RAR: a D Company harbour was attacked on 2 March during its in-country training, killing two, and on 20 March a platoon commander was mortally wounded clearing a bunker system. On 31 March a platoon of 2 RAR, under 3 RAR's command, ran into the headquarters of D445 Battalion and lost two killed, one an RAAF crewman, before withdrawing. The record counts 7 killed on the Task Force's side and 19 wounded, and 31 enemy killed.

1971-04.summary: 2 RAR's last full month, in Phoi Hop, and 3 RAR in Briar Patch; two Australians killed when a medical evacuation helicopter was shot down.
1971-04.text: 2 RAR (16 contacts) in Phoi Hop and 3 RAR (16) in Briar Patch shared the month's work, much of it security, ambushes and patrols; on 20 April 2 RAR platoons twice met D445 Battalion men in bunker systems. On 17 April a medical evacuation helicopter came to a Regional Force company that had struck a mine; it was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade and crashed on the evacuation party, which advisers of the Australian Army Training Team Vietnam were supervising, killing two Australians, an American and a Vietnamese. The record counts 2 killed on the Task Force's side and 8 wounded, and 10 enemy killed.

1971-05.summary: A quiet month as 4 RAR relieved 2 RAR: Briar Patch ended, SAS patrols ambushed, and carriers struck mines around Cam My.
1971-05.text: A quiet month, with 24 contacts, as Briar Patch came to an end (4 contacts). The Special Air Service was in contact most often (6): on 19 May a patrol ambushed and killed four enemy, possibly of 274 Regiment. Carriers of A Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, struck anti-tank mines in and near the Cam My rubber on 2 and 24 May. On 22 May HMAS Sydney landed 4 RAR at Vung Tau and took 2 RAR home[1]. The record counts 5 wounded on the Task Force's side and 7 enemy killed.

1971-06.summary: Overlord on the Long Khanh border, with the Battle of Long Khanh and a carrier destroyed, then 4 RAR's Hermit Park.
1971-06.text: Overlord (22 contacts) took the Task Force north to the Long Khanh border to stop the enemy gaining a foothold in Phuoc Tuy[1]. On 7 June 3 RAR fought the Battle of Long Khanh against a bunker system of the 3rd Battalion, 33rd North Vietnamese Regiment, and on 12 June a carrier of A Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment, exploded when a rocket-propelled grenade set off the claymores it carried, killing eight. 4 RAR's Hermit Park (22) followed, with a cavalry ambush on 21 June that killed 12 enemy and fighting at a bunker system of 274 Regiment on 25 June. The record counts 12 killed on the Task Force's side and 29 wounded, the heaviest month of the year, and 38 enemy killed.

sources.title: Australians in Operation Overlord and the Battle of Long Khanh in 1971

1971-07.summary: Hermit Park ended; 3 RAR in Hawker and 4 RAR in Iron Fox, attacking bunkers of 274 Regiment with tanks.
1971-07.text: Hermit Park ran on to late July (16 contacts), mostly small ambushes by 4 RAR (16 contacts in all), while 3 RAR (9) worked in Hawker (6). At the month's end 4 RAR began Iron Fox against the 1st Battalion, 274 Regiment: on 29 July a platoon of C Company withdrew from a bunker system with three wounded, and on 30 July D Company, with tanks of C Squadron, 1st Armoured Regiment, cleared a nine-bunker system, one Australian being killed and 12 enemy. The record counts 1 killed on the Task Force's side and 13 wounded, and 30 enemy killed.

1971-08.summary: The announcement that the Task Force would leave by the end of the year; small operations and SAS ambushes against 274 Regiment and D445 Battalion.
1971-08.text: On 18 August the Prime Minister, William McMahon, announced that the rest of the Task Force would be withdrawn at the end of the year[1]. The work went on in smaller operations: 4 RAR's North Ward (7 contacts) and 3 RAR's Inverbrackie (3), where platoons met D445 Battalion in bunkers along the Song Hoa. On 13 August a Special Air Service patrol ambushed part of the headquarters of the 3rd Battalion, 274 Regiment, and one of the dead was the regiment's deputy chief of staff. The record counts 4 wounded on the Task Force's side and 13 enemy killed.

sources.title: Withdrawal of Australian personnel from Vietnam War 1971 to 1973

1971-09.summary: The Battle of Nui Le in Operation Ivanhoe, the last major battle Australians fought in Vietnam.
1971-09.text: With the tanks gone home in mid-September, the North Vietnamese 33rd Regiment tried to establish itself in Phuoc Tuy, and 4 RAR led Operation Ivanhoe to stop it[1]. On 21 September, in the Battle of Nui Le, D Company assaulted a bunker system of the regiment's 3rd Battalion and five Australians were killed, while B Company was mortared and had 15 wounded. Before that, 4 RAR's North Ward (7 contacts) and 3 RAR's Cudlee Creek (3) had continued the month's ambushes and searches. The record counts 5 killed on the Task Force's side and 29 wounded, and 34 enemy killed.

sources.title: Operation Ivanhoe and the Battle of Nui Le 1971

1971-10.summary: The withdrawal began: 3 RAR went home, while 4 RAR and the cavalry kept up the province's security.
1971-10.text: 3 RAR's vehicles were loaded onto HMAS Sydney at Vung Tau on 6 October, the first major move in the withdrawal, and the battalion went home that month[1]. The 10 contacts are mostly security (6), by the carriers of the 3rd Cavalry Regiment (5) and 4 RAR (2) in South Ward. On 1 October the village of Ngai Giao, with its Popular Force platoon, was attacked by 50 to 60 enemy, who withdrew after the carriers and artillery joined in. The record counts one wounded, a Popular Force soldier at Ngai Giao, and 3 enemy killed.

sources.title: Withdrawal of Australian personnel from Vietnam War 1971 to 1973

1971-11.summary: The last contact, on 2 November, and the last battalion's departure from Nui Dat on 7 November 1971.
1971-11.text: The record's last contact came on 2 November, when 5 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR, was fired on by two or three enemy, with no casualties. The last battalion left Nui Dat on 7 November[1]. 4 RAR went home in December, and most Australian combat troops were home by the end of the year[2].

sources.title: Withdrawal of Australian personnel from Vietnam War 1971 to 1973
